output.situation: The user freelances, and income swings between great months and almost empty ones. They want a way to budget without knowing what they will earn. The decisive unknown is whether even their emptiest month covers fixed bills such as rent, insurance, and loans. Their goals and constraints are not given. The sources were not checked online here, so every basis is unverified and the ideas are paraphrased. The three minds below are fictional.

minds.title: The Slack Keeper
minds.concern: Thin cash drains attention, so a plan must leave breathing room before it asks for discipline.
minds.author: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir
minds.book: Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much

minds.title: The Cash-Flow Sorter
minds.concern: Rules that act automatically when money arrives beat good intentions, and each payment should be divided before it can be spent.
minds.author: Mike Michalowicz

minds.title: The Uncertainty Realist
minds.concern: Unknowable income should not be treated as a measurable average, so plans must be built on defensible floors and judgment.
minds.author: Frank H. Knight

debate.speaker: The Slack Keeper
debate.text: Here is my reading: the hard part is not the spreadsheet, it is the empty month. When money runs short, worry about rent takes over the mind and crowds out planning, so a budget that works only when someone is calm fails exactly when it is needed. Slack, not precision, is the real asset.
debate.author: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir
debate.book: Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much
debate.basis: [Basis: Mullainathan and Shafir, Scarcity, the bandwidth and slack ideas; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Cash-Flow Sorter
debate.text: The Slack Keeper says the real problem is the empty month and the worry it brings. I say the how is mechanical. Every payment is split on arrival by fixed percentages into taxes, bills, profit, and a pay account, and the owner pays themselves a steady wage on a set date. Rules beat willpower.
debate.author: Mike Michalowicz
debate.basis: [Basis: Michalowicz, Profit First, the account-allocation system; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Uncertainty Realist
debate.text: The Cash-Flow Sorter says percentages on arrival solve it. They assume the stream resembles its past. Knight separated risk, which can be counted from repeated cases, from uncertainty, which cannot. Spring 2020 shows it: freelancers whose events were cancelled had years of records that predicted nothing. Plan around the worst plausible stretch, not an average.
debate.author: Frank H. Knight
debate.basis: [Basis: Knight, Risk, Uncertainty and Profit, the risk versus uncertainty distinction; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Slack Keeper
debate.text: I accept the floor idea, but a floor on paper pays no rent. Sugarcane farmers in India, paid once a year, scored worse on thinking tests before harvest than after, which suggests thin cash itself drains the mind. The user said some months are almost empty, so maybe those months feel like a threat, and if so a buffer buys calm, not only cash.
debate.author: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir
debate.book: Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much
debate.basis: [Basis: Mullainathan and Shafir, Scarcity, the sugarcane farmer study and slack; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Cash-Flow Sorter
debate.text: The Slack Keeper reads the empty months as a threat that a buffer would calm. I reject that, because a buffer takes a year to build and a rule takes a day. A rival reading: the user said some months are great, so perhaps spending rises to match them, and if so splitting each payment fixes the whiplash faster than saving.
debate.author: Mike Michalowicz
debate.basis: [Basis: Michalowicz, Profit First, paying yourself a fixed wage and small-plate habits; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Uncertainty Realist
debate.text: Both readings might be true, and that is the cost. The user may want to spend freely in the great months and also feel safe in the empty ones, and they cannot fully have both. A high pay line serves the first. A low floor with a thick buffer serves the second. A JPMorgan Chase Institute study of bank data found household income swinging widely month to month, so this tension is common.
debate.author: Frank H. Knight
debate.basis: [Basis: Knight, Risk, Uncertainty and Profit, uncertainty and the limits of averaging; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Cash-Flow Sorter
debate.text: I drop my claim that fixed percentages on every payment are enough. The Uncertainty Realist's point that a few good months say little about the next ones moved me. I now hold something narrower: set a low fixed wage first, and use the percentages only on what arrives above it.
debate.author: Mike Michalowicz
debate.basis: [Basis: Michalowicz, Profit First, owner's pay and allocation percentages; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Slack Keeper
debate.text: The Cash-Flow Sorter now sets a low wage first and splits the surplus. That depends on a fact the user has not given: whether even the emptiest month covers fixed bills like rent, insurance, and loans. If it does, wage first works and a small buffer will do. If it does not, the first job is cutting fixed costs or building buffer, and percentages should wait.
debate.author: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir
debate.book: Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much
debate.basis: [Basis: Mullainathan and Shafir, Scarcity, slack as protection against shortfall; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Uncertainty Realist
debate.text: The Slack Keeper puts buffer ahead of percentages when the worst month falls short. I add what could be lost. With no cushion, a person might take a bad client or underprice out of fear, which costs the freedom to say no, perhaps the point of freelancing. If that is the real concern, buffer comes before any steady wage. I go further than Knight here.
debate.author: Frank H. Knight
debate.basis: [Basis: Knight, Risk, Uncertainty and Profit, bearing uncertainty and judgment; the extension is my own; source not verified, no link]

debate.speaker: The Cash-Flow Sorter
debate.text: The Uncertainty Realist wants buffer before any steady wage, even when bills are covered. I still say pay the wage first and let the buffer grow from the surplus, because a wage trains a person to live below the good months. Maybe the longest empty stretch decides it: if lean runs last two or three months, I lose; if they are single months, I keep my order.
debate.author: Mike Michalowicz
debate.basis: [Basis: Michalowicz, Profit First, pay yourself first and the surplus accounts; source not verified, no link]

output.clearer: The main insight is that the question is really two problems: how to divide money that arrives unevenly, and how to live with not knowing how much will arrive. A low fixed wage with percentages on the surplus handles the first, and a buffer sized to the worst plausible stretch handles the second. What stays disputed is the order: wage first with the buffer growing from surplus, or buffer first even when bills are covered. One possible self-reflection: how much of the dread is about the empty months themselves, and how much is about spending that rises in the great months? This is a possibility, not a conclusion about the user.
output.dependsOn: If the emptiest month still covers fixed bills, a low fixed wage with percentages on the surplus becomes more reasonable, because the floor is safe and the buffer can grow gradually. If the emptiest month falls short of fixed bills, cutting fixed costs and building a buffer becomes more reasonable first, because no percentage rule can create money that is not there. If the main worry is losing the freedom to refuse bad clients, a buffer before a steady wage looks stronger, because desperation is what that loss would feel like. If the longest empty stretch is unknown, a proportionate way to learn it is to list income by month for the past one to two years, note the longest run below fixed bills, and note whether the lean months follow a seasonal pattern.
